why: Unauthorised geofence modification can enable restricted-airspace entry, propagate into flight authorisation, and create serious safety consequences.
Centralised telemetry poisoning can corrupt multiple mandatory services simultaneously, creating widespread operational and potentially catastrophic safety failures.
Manipulated weather and traffic feeds can produce unsafe routing decisions and compromise multiple safety-relevant information services.
Audit destruction undermines incident reconstruction and mandatory compliance evidence, although its direct safety consequence is limited.
Credential compromise enables scalable operational data exfiltration and potentially affects all dependent services, with limited direct safety impact.
Database compromise can corrupt or expose extensive operational records and disrupt dependent services, requiring substantial recovery effort.
Compromised enforcement records undermine regulatory accountability across the ecosystem, although no direct aircraft safety pathway is specified.
Regulatory ambiguity can systematically weaken cybersecurity governance across all layers, with indirect but substantial safety implications.
Strategic document theft provides adversarial intelligence and compromises confidentiality, but the stated scenario lacks a direct safety consequence.
GNSS spoofing or jamming can directly compromise aircraft positioning, cause restricted-airspace incursions, and create collision or loss-of-aircraft scenarios.
C2 disruption can remove aircraft control during BVLOS operations, creating uncontrolled flight, collision, and potentially catastrophic consequences.
Persistent flight-controller compromise can subvert aircraft behaviour, propagate malicious telemetry, and plausibly cause aircraft loss.
Power or battery-management compromise can cause ground-station outages or uncontrolled landings, with significant physical safety consequences.
Manipulated altitude, positioning, or inertial measurements can directly corrupt flight decisions and plausibly cause aircraft crashes.
Physical compromise of vertiport control facilities can disrupt landing operations and create serious risks for aircraft and people.
Trusted supply-chain compromise can distribute persistent malicious firmware across fleets, enabling widespread and difficult-to-detect aircraft subversion.
Identity spoofing enables unauthorised and unaccountable operations, weakening regulatory compliance and operator accountability.
False aircraft positions can conceal real conflicts, corrupt shared situational awareness, and directly undermine collision-avoidance decisions.
Authorisation bypass can permit illegal conflicting flights and restricted-airspace access, compromising fundamental U-Space safety controls.
Gateway flooding can disable mandatory services across an entire operational volume, interrupting authorisations and service continuity.
Falsified geofences can authorise unsafe routing into restricted airspace and propagate incorrect information into dependent services.
